meta.blurb: Isla Marlowe's phone rings in a kitchen drawer and her supper goes cold. Her workshop clock has stopped at twenty to ten, and the town whispers about her husband. Her sister Hannah remembers a childhood game, and starts looking for a clue.
meta.bible: Hannah Reed: Isla's younger sister, a schoolteacher, clever and loyal, our point of view. Isla Marlowe: a clock restorer who works for Gideon Pryce; maiden name Reed. Owen Marlowe: Isla's husband, a quiet accountant. Gideon Pryce: owner of Pryce Antiques, silver hair, smooth voice; sells stolen clocks with forged papers. Mabel Cray: Pryce's frightened young assistant. Inspector Dana Okoye: the calm police detective. Mr Doyle: the old neighbour who saw the green van. Reverend Joan Bright: the vicar of Saint Brannock's church. Miss Agnes Penhale: Isla's old teacher, who lives on Gull Island near the lighthouse. Sam Tully: the old ferryman. Saltmere: the small seaside town. Gull Island: reached by the last ferry, which leaves at twenty to ten. Anchor Lane: where Isla's father's old workshop stands. Thornby: the village beyond which Pryce rents a barn. Lantern Festival: the town's night of paper lanterns, postponed by a week. Saint Brannock's: the church whose turret clock was stolen last April. Facts: the workshop clock was stopped at twenty to ten, the ferry time; the childhood game was that the time on a clock stands for a place; the green van has a pale stripe; the red scarf was knitted by Hannah; Owen was saving cash to buy back the old workshop. Voice and tone: tense, warm and clear, a fair-play mystery; no violence or gore; Isla is alive and Pryce is arrested.

A1A2: Hannah got off the train in Saltmere to visit her sister Isla.
Owen met her at the station and said Isla was still working.
Isla did not come home, and her phone was in the kitchen.
Her workshop was empty, and the old clock on the table had stopped.
At midnight Owen called the police, and Hannah could not sleep.
In the morning Inspector Okoye came and asked many careful questions.
The inspector asked if Isla was happy, and Hannah did not know.
Men found Isla's red scarf on the sea wall by the water.
The town newspaper had Isla's face on the front page.
Hannah went to the shop where Isla worked, full of old things.
A young woman in the shop said Isla had been very upset.
In the workshop, Hannah found a little book full of numbers.
The police found that Owen had taken much money from the bank.
Hannah asked Owen about the money, but he would not answer.
A neighbour said he saw a green van near the workshop.
Hannah remembered a game she and Isla played as children.
Newspaper people stood outside the house, and Owen closed the curtains.
Hannah opened the stopped clock and found a small brass key.
The key opened a small cupboard under the work table.
One number belonged to a clock stolen from the town church.
The inspector looked and said it was not enough yet.
The vicar said Mr Pryce once wanted to buy the church clock.
Behind Pryce's shop, Hannah saw a green van with a stripe.
That night a thief came into the workshop and took everything.
Owen told Hannah the money was for a surprise for Isla.
The lawyer said Owen's story was true, and the inspector listened.
On the wall, a paper said the last boat left at twenty to ten.
Hannah understood Isla's game: the clock showed the island ferry.
The boat man remembered a woman in a grey hood on Friday.
Owen sent a message to the inspector, and they decided to go.
The boat crossed the grey sea to a small island.
Smoke rose from a small stone cottage near the lighthouse.
An old woman opened the door and smiled at them.
Isla was alive, and Owen held her tightly.
Isla said Mr Pryce sold stolen clocks, and he was angry.
Isla said she hid on purpose, and she was very sorry.
Isla showed them a brass plate from the church clock.
In town, Mabel told Mr Pryce where Hannah had gone.
Mr Pryce knocked on the cottage door and smiled at them.
Isla kept him talking while Hannah went quietly out the back.
In the lighthouse, Hannah found the big lamp and turned it on.
The police saw the light and came across the water.
Mr Pryce saw the light and ran for his boat.
Owen stood on the narrow boards, and Mr Pryce slipped and fell.
The police boat came, and the inspector arrested Mr Pryce.
Mabel told the police she had helped Mr Pryce, and she cried.

B1B2: Hannah steps off the evening train in Saltmere, a small town by the sea. She has come to spend the Lantern Festival weekend with her sister Isla, whom she has not seen for a year.
Owen is waiting by the gate, looking tired, and he takes her bag without a word. He says that Isla is finishing an old clock at her workshop and will be home soon.
They waited for Isla until the soup was cold, and then Owen tried her number. A phone began to ring inside a kitchen drawer, and neither of them said anything for a moment.
The workshop door is unlocked and the lamp is still burning, but there is no sign of Isla. On her bench stands a tall clock whose hands have stopped at twenty to ten.
At midnight Owen telephones the police, and his voice shakes as he gives his wife's name. Hannah lies awake in the spare room, listening for the sound of a key in the front door.
Inspector Dana Okoye arrives at eight, a calm woman with a worn notebook and sharp, patient eyes. She asks Owen to describe, minute by minute, the last time he saw his wife.
Outside in the garden, the inspector asks Hannah whether her sister and Owen were happy together. Hannah wants to say yes at once, but she remembers the strange tone of Isla's last letter.
Volunteers search the harbour all morning, and one of them finds Isla's red scarf lying on the sea wall. The news spreads through the town before noon, and everyone begins to fear the worst.

By Saturday morning Isla's photograph is on the front of the local paper, and everyone in the cafe is whispering. Some people say that the husband is always the one to blame, and Hannah has to leave the room.
Hannah visits the antique shop where Isla works, a dim room full of clocks and china. Its owner, Gideon Pryce, is smooth and sorry, and he says Isla left at five as usual.

When Pryce goes into the back room, the shop assistant Mabel Cray whispers to Hannah. She says that on Friday Isla had been upset about some numbers in an old book, and then she stops, looking frightened.
That evening Hannah searches the workshop and finds a small notebook taped under a drawer. Every page is covered in long numbers, each with a date beside it, and none of it makes sense to her.
Inspector Okoye learns that Owen has taken a large amount of cash out of the bank over six months. She asks him, without any anger, what the money was for, and he says only that it is private.
Hannah asks Owen directly about the money, and he turns away to the window. He says that he would never hurt Isla, and that she must simply trust him.
Old Mr Doyle, who lives opposite the workshop, tells the police that he saw a green van in the lane on Friday. It was parked there at dusk, and he did not see who got into it.
Lying awake, Hannah remembers a game she and Isla played when they were small. Whoever hid would leave a clue, and the other would have to read it from the hands of a clock.
Reporters gather outside the house, and the town begins to say that Owen is hiding something. He closes the curtains and tells Hannah that nobody is going to believe him.
Late at night Hannah returns to the workshop and opens the back of the stopped clock. Taped inside the case, behind the weights, is a small brass key that does not belong to the clock.
The key fits a narrow cabinet beneath the workbench, and inside lie dozens of photographs. They show the brass plates of old clocks, each one marked with a maker's name and a long number.
Among the photographs is a newspaper cutting about a church clock stolen last spring. Its maker's number is the very first one written in Isla's notebook, and Hannah feels her mouth go dry.

Inspector Okoye studies the pictures on Hannah's phone for a long time and says they are interesting, but they are not proof. She tells Hannah to leave the investigation to the police and not to go anywhere alone.
At Saint Brannock's, the vicar, Reverend Joan Bright, shows Hannah the empty room in the tower. She says that Gideon Pryce had offered to buy the old clock only a month before it vanished.
On her way back, Hannah looks into the yard behind Pryce's shop. There, half hidden under a sheet, stands a green van with a pale stripe along its side.

That night someone breaks into the workshop while Hannah hides behind a curtain. The person, wearing gloves, takes every photograph and the notebook, but Hannah has already photographed them with her phone.
At last Owen breaks his silence and shows Hannah a letter from a lawyer. He has been saving money in secret to buy back Isla's father's old workshop, as a surprise for their tenth anniversary.
Inspector Okoye telephones the lawyer, who confirms every word of Owen's story. She tells Hannah quietly that Owen is no longer her main worry, although she still cannot say where Isla is.
While Owen makes tea, Hannah studies the ferry timetable pinned beside the window. The last boat to Gull Island on festival eve leaves at twenty to ten, exactly the time on the stopped clock.
Suddenly the old game makes sense: in it, the time on the clock always stood for a place. Isla has stopped the clock at the ferry time to tell her sister that she has gone to Gull Island.
At the harbour, the old ferryman Sam Tully remembers a woman in a grey hood on the last boat on Friday. She paid in cash, kept her face down and did not come back with him.
Hannah and Owen decide to take the first ferry in the morning and go to the island themselves. Owen sends a short message to Inspector Okoye so that someone knows where they are.
The ferry rolls across the grey water, and cold spray stings Hannah's face. Ahead of them rises Gull Island, a long green hump with a white lighthouse standing at its far end.
Beside the lighthouse they find a stone cottage with smoke curling from its chimney. It belongs to Miss Agnes Penhale, who taught Isla at school and has lived on the island for forty years.
The door opens, and a small old woman in a green cardigan looks up at them calmly. “I wondered how long you would take,” she says, and steps aside to let them in.
Isla is standing in the lamplit kitchen, thinner and paler but alive, with tears on her face. Owen crosses the room in two steps and holds her as though he will never let go.

Isla explains that Gideon Pryce has been selling stolen clocks with false papers, and that she found out by chance. When she asked him about it on Friday, his kindness vanished and he warned her to be quiet.

Isla says she decided to vanish so that Pryce would think she was gone while she gathered proof. She left the scarf and the stopped clock for Hannah alone, and she never guessed the police would blame Owen.
On the table Isla places a flat brass plate and a thin folder. The plate came from the stolen church clock, and the folder holds copies of pages from Pryce's secret account book.
Meanwhile, back in Saltmere, a frightened Mabel Cray tells Pryce that Hannah and Owen have taken the morning ferry. Pryce says nothing for a moment, and then he reaches for his coat.
There is a polite knock at the cottage door, and Gideon Pryce stands outside with rain dripping from his hat. He smiles and says that he has only come to take his clever clockmaker home.
Isla keeps Pryce talking about clocks and old makers, and he is vain enough to enjoy it. While he talks, Hannah slips out of the back door and runs through the rain toward the lighthouse.
Inside the lighthouse Hannah climbs a long spiral stair and finds the great lamp under its glass. She pulls the heavy lever, and a bright beam sweeps out across the stormy water.

Inspector Okoye has been waiting with a police boat ever since she received Owen's message. When the lighthouse beam flashes through the storm, she knows that it is the signal, and the launch roars away from the harbour.
Pryce sees the beam sweeping across the water and understands at once what it means. He snatches the brass plate from the table and runs toward his motorboat at the jetty.
Owen reaches the jetty first and plants himself on the narrow boards. Pryce rushes at him, slips on the wet planks and drops the brass plate, which clangs onto the stones.
The police launch comes alongside the jetty, and Inspector Okoye steps ashore in her dripping coat. She looks at the brass plate, then at Pryce, and she arrests him on suspicion of theft and fraud.

Back in Saltmere, Mabel Cray sits in the police station and confesses everything. She admits that she carried boxes for Pryce and kept quiet because she was afraid, and she promises to tell the court the whole truth.
Using Mabel's information, the police search a barn that Pryce rents outside town. Under blankets in the corner they find the great turret clock of Saint Brannock's, safe and almost undamaged.
Back at home, Owen tells Isla the truth about the missing money and gives her the iron key. She stares at it, then at him, and then begins to laugh and cry at once.
At sunrise the sisters sit on the sea wall with the red scarf between them. They promise each other that, whatever happens in the future, neither of them will keep a secret again.

A week late, the Lantern Festival finally lights the harbour with hundreds of paper lanterns. As the crowd gasps, the restored clock of Saint Brannock's strikes ten, and Isla, Owen and Hannah smile at each other.
C1C2: The evening train set Hannah down at Saltmere just as the lamps along the harbour began to glow, and the smell of salt and frying fish drifted over the platform. She had come for the Lantern Festival, the town's great night of paper lights, and for the sister she had not properly talked to in a year. Isla's last letter had sounded cheerful, yet something in its careful phrasing had stayed with Hannah the whole way from the city.

Her brother-in-law Owen was waiting beside the ticket office, a quiet man in a tidy coat who always seemed to be thinking about something else. He took her bag with his usual courtesy and explained that Isla was still at her workshop, finishing the repair of an old clock before the festival began. Hannah noticed that he did not quite meet her eyes, and she put it down to the long day.

Supper had been laid for three, with candles and the good plates, but by nine o'clock the soup had gone cold and the third chair was still empty. When Owen finally rang his wife's number, a muffled buzzing rose from the kitchen drawer, where her phone lay switched on and quite alone. Isla, who carried that phone everywhere, had left it behind, and the silence that followed seemed to Hannah louder than the ringing.

Isla's workshop stood at the end of a cobbled lane, and its door swung open at the first touch, with a lamp still burning above the bench. Tools lay in neat rows, a cup of tea had gone cold, and in the centre of the table a tall clock stood silent, its hands frozen at twenty to ten. Of Isla herself there was no trace, and Hannah felt the first cold finger of real fear.

Just before midnight Owen telephoned the police, speaking in the stiff, careful voice of a man who is trying very hard not to break. Hannah lay awake in the spare room, listening to the sea and straining for the sound of a key turning in the front door. None came, and the hours dragged past, as slow and heavy as a tide that refuses to turn.

Inspector Dana Okoye arrived at eight the next morning, a calm and unhurried woman with a worn notebook and eyes that seemed to weigh every answer. She asked Owen to describe, minute by minute, the last time he had seen his wife, and she wrote down even his pauses. Hannah, watching from the doorway, had the uneasy feeling that the inspector was listening just as hard to what he left out.

In the garden, away from Owen, the inspector asked Hannah whether her sister's marriage had been a happy one. Hannah opened her mouth to say yes, but the memory of Isla's last letter, so bright on the surface and so strangely guarded underneath, held the word back. It was the first time she had admitted to herself that she had not been told everything.

By midday volunteers in oilskins had searched the beaches, the harbour and the cliff path, and it was on the sea wall that one of them found a red woollen scarf. Hannah recognised it at once, for she had knitted it herself, badly, for Isla's birthday six years before. The word spread through Saltmere in minutes, and with it came the whispered fear that the sea had taken her.

By Saturday morning Isla's smiling photograph filled the front page of the local paper, and in the harbour café every conversation dropped to a murmur as Hannah came in. She heard it distinctly from a corner table: the husband, someone said, is always the one who knows. Burning with anger on Owen's behalf, and with a small, shameful doubt of her own, she walked out into the wind.

The shop where Isla mended clocks stood on the main street, a dim, crowded place that smelled of beeswax and old brass. Its owner, Gideon Pryce, received Hannah with silver hair, soft hands and a manner of well-oiled sympathy, assuring her that Isla had left at five as she always did. Everything he said was kind and reasonable, and yet Hannah noticed that he never once asked where Isla might be.

While Pryce disappeared into the back room to find a card, his young assistant, Mabel Cray, leaned across the counter and spoke in a rapid whisper. On Friday afternoon, she said, Isla had been upset about some numbers in an old account book, and had asked a question that Mr Pryce did not like. Before she could say more, a floorboard creaked in the doorway, and Mabel became absorbed in polishing a teapot.

That evening, alone in the workshop, Hannah searched every drawer until her fingers found a slim notebook taped to the underside of the lowest one. Its pages were crowded with long numbers in Isla's tidy hand, each followed by a date, a place and a small tick, though nothing in them explained itself. Whatever her sister had been counting, she had plainly not wanted it to be found.

Within two days the inspector's team had examined the couple's bank accounts and discovered that Owen had withdrawn a large sum in cash, in small amounts, over the last six months. When she asked him, politely and without raising her voice, what the money had been for, he stared at his hands and answered only that it was private. In that moment, whether she wished it or not, the quiet accountant became the most interesting man in Saltmere.

That night Hannah faced him across the kitchen table and asked, as gently as she could, where the money had gone. Owen rose, crossed to the window and stood with his back to her for so long that she thought he would never speak. When he did, he said only that he would never harm Isla and that Hannah would simply have to trust him, a request she found harder with every passing hour.

Old Mr Doyle, who lived opposite the workshop and rarely missed anything in the lane, told the police that a green van had been parked there at dusk on Friday. He had not seen the driver, he admitted, because the television had called him indoors, but he remembered a pale stripe along its side. The inspector wrote this down with great care, though Hannah could see that she had no more idea than anyone whose van it was.

Late that night, unable to sleep, Hannah found herself remembering a game she and Isla had played as little girls in their father's workshop. Whoever hid would leave one clue behind, and the seeker had to read the answer from the hands of an old clock, so that the time on the face became a place, and a place became a promise. She had not thought of it in twenty years, and she did not yet dare to believe it might matter.

By Monday a small crowd of reporters had gathered outside the gate, calling Owen's name and shining cameras at the windows. He drew the curtains one by one, and the gloom that settled over the house seemed to thicken with every hour. “Nobody believes me,” he said quietly, and Hannah, who herself had begun to wonder, felt ashamed.

Convinced that the stopped clock was no accident, Hannah slipped into the workshop after midnight and unscrewed the back of its tall case. Behind the dusty weights, fixed to the wood with a strip of tape, she found a small brass key that plainly belonged to no part of the mechanism. Her heart began to race, for she knew her sister's habits, and Isla never hid anything without meaning someone to look.

The key turned smoothly in a narrow cabinet beneath the workbench, a door Hannah had taken for part of the panelling. Inside lay a thick folder of photographs, each showing the brass maker's plate of a different antique clock, with its name, its date and its long, stamped number. She recognised the numbers at once, for they were the same ones that crowded the pages of the hidden notebook.

Beneath the photographs lay a yellowing cutting from the previous April, reporting the theft of the great turret clock of Saint Brannock's church. The maker's number printed in that article matched the first entry in Isla's notebook, and so, Hannah found with growing dread, did a dozen others on the list. Her sister had not been counting numbers at all; she had been tracing stolen things, and Hannah photographed every page with trembling hands.

Inspector Okoye examined the pictures on Hannah's phone for a long time, drawing each page closer with one careful finger, and then sat back with a sigh. Interesting, she said, certainly, but numbers and pictures were not proof of a crime, and they proved nothing at all about where Isla had gone. She asked Hannah, firmly and with some kindness, to leave the investigating to the police and never to go anywhere alone.

In the tower of Saint Brannock's, the vicar, Reverend Joan Bright, led Hannah up a spiral stair to a bare room where the great clock had once ticked. She explained that the church had refused every offer to buy it, though the most generous had come from Mr Gideon Pryce just a month before it vanished. A tall man had dismantled and removed the clock in a single night, the vicar added, and no one had heard a sound.

On her way back from the church Hannah took a different road and found herself in the lane behind Pryce Antiques, where a high gate stood slightly ajar. In the yard beyond, half hidden under a loose sheet, a green van waited with a pale stripe running along its side, exactly as Mr Doyle had described. She did not stay to look more closely, but she walked home with her pulse hammering.

Hannah had gone back to the workshop to watch and wait, and she was crouching behind a curtain when the lock clicked and a gloved hand pushed open the door. A tall figure swept the cabinet bare, snatching the folder, the notebook and the cutting, and then slipped away into the night without a word. Hannah, shaking, remembered with a rush of relief that every page was safe on her phone.

Shaken by the break-in, Owen finally abandoned his silence and laid a lawyer's letter on the kitchen table, together with a heavy iron key. For six months, he confessed, he had been saving every spare coin to buy back the old workshop on Anchor Lane that had belonged to Isla's father, and he had meant to give it to her on their anniversary. He had kept it secret so long, he said wretchedly, that the secret had turned into a cage.

Inspector Okoye spent an hour on the telephone with the lawyer in Anchor Lane, and every detail of Owen's story was confirmed down to the last signature. She told Hannah, with the faint air of a woman revising a theory, that Owen was no longer her chief concern. Yet nothing about that comfort brought Isla any closer, and the question of where she had gone remained as heavy as ever.

While Owen made tea, Hannah's gaze drifted to the ferry timetable that hung beside the kitchen window, its corners curled from years of damp. The last boat to Gull Island on the eve of the festival, she read, left the harbour at twenty to ten, which was precisely the hour at which the workshop clock had stopped. She felt a jolt run through her, as though someone had opened a door in a wall she had been leaning against.

Suddenly the old game made perfect sense, for in it the time on the clock had always stood for a place, and the place was always where the hider waited. Isla had stopped her clock at the hour of the last ferry, and she had left it in plain view of no one but a sister who would remember how to read it. Hannah was almost afraid to breathe, because if she was right, Isla had been alive and thinking all along.

At first light Hannah found the old ferryman, Sam Tully, coiling a rope on the harbour steps, and she described her sister as well as she could. He scratched his chin and remembered a woman in a grey hood who had taken the last boat on Friday, paid in cash and kept her face turned to the water. She had never come back on the return trip, he said, and he had wondered about her ever since.

They agreed to cross to Gull Island on the first ferry of the morning, and Owen, remembering the inspector's warning, sent her a short message so that someone would know where they had gone. The wind had risen in the night, and clouds were stacking up over the sea like dark furniture. Neither of them said that they were afraid, but both of them kept looking at the sky.

The ferry rolled out across the grey water, and cold spray flung itself over the rail and stung Hannah's cheeks as she gazed ahead. Gull Island rose slowly out of the haze, a long green hump of rock and grass with a white lighthouse standing guard at its farthest end. Beside her Owen gripped the rail with both hands, and she saw that his knuckles were white.

Beside the lighthouse stood a low stone cottage with a thread of smoke rising from its chimney and a vegetable patch fenced against the wind. It belonged, Hannah remembered, to Miss Agnes Penhale, who had taught Isla at school and had retired to the island some forty years before. She knocked, and for a long moment there was no sound but the gulls.

The door opened at last, and a small, upright old woman in a green cardigan looked from one face to the other with perfect composure. “I wondered how long you would take,” she said, in the tone of a teacher addressing two late pupils, and she stepped aside to let them pass. Hannah's heart gave a great bound, for she understood from the old woman's calm that they had been expected for some time.

In the lamplit kitchen at the back of the cottage stood Isla, thinner and paler than before, with her hair cut short and her eyes brimming with tears. Owen crossed the room in two strides and wrapped her in his arms as though he could never again bear to let go, while Hannah laughed and wept at the same moment. It was a minute before anyone could speak, and when they could, nobody was able to say anything sensible.

Over tea, Isla explained that her employer, Gideon Pryce, had for years been selling stolen antique clocks with forged papers, and that she had discovered it by chance while repairing a clock whose number she recognised. When she had questioned him on Friday afternoon, his smooth kindness had vanished, and he had warned her in a very quiet voice that clever women who talked too much tended to lose everything. She had understood in that instant that she would never be safe in Saltmere while he believed she knew.

She had decided in a single desperate hour to vanish, Isla said, so that Pryce would believe her frightened into silence while she secured the proof that would end his crimes. She had left her phone behind because he had been reading her messages, and she had left the clock stopped at the ferry hour for the one person alive who would know how to read it. What she had never foreseen, she added with a stricken look at Owen, was that the police and the whole town might suspect her own husband.

From beneath a loose floorboard Isla drew out a flat brass plate, tarnished and engraved, and laid beside it a thin folder tied with string. The plate, she said, had been taken from the stolen turret clock of Saint Brannock's, and the folder contained photocopies of Pryce's private accounts, which listed every theft and every buyer. Together, she believed, they were more than enough to bring his long and quiet trade in stolen treasures to an end.

Meanwhile, in the shop in Saltmere, Pryce had been quietly collecting information, and the trembling Mabel Cray told him that Hannah had been asking questions and that the ferryman had seen a woman in a grey hood. She stammered out that the Marlowes had taken the morning boat to Gull Island, and then she wished at once that she had kept her mouth shut. Pryce said nothing, but his soft face hardened, and he reached silently for his coat as the first storm clouds gathered over the sea.

Just after two o'clock there came a polite knock at the cottage door, and when Miss Penhale opened it, Gideon Pryce stood on the step with rain dripping from his hat and a courteous smile on his face. He had only come, he said gently, to take his most gifted clockmaker home, and to collect a small piece of property that she had borrowed. His voice was warm and his manner perfectly friendly, but the pale eyes above the smile were as cold as the rain on the glass.

Isla, who knew his weakness, began to talk about old clockmakers and their secrets, and Pryce, who could never resist an audience for his learning, was soon holding forth with relish. While his attention was fixed upon her, Hannah slid silently through the back door and ran through the rain toward the lighthouse, her coat streaming behind her. If the old lamp still worked, Miss Penhale had whispered as she passed, someone on the mainland might see it.

Hannah climbed the lighthouse stair two steps at a time, her breath burning, until she reached the lantern room where a great glass lens stood dusty under its cover. She wrenched off the cloth and threw the heavy lever, and with a groan of old machinery the beam leaped out, a bar of white light sweeping the dark water. Far below, the sea seemed to catch fire with it, and she prayed that somebody was watching.

Inspector Okoye had been waiting at the harbour with a police launch ever since Owen's message had reached her, uncertain whether to trust a hunch against the coming storm. When the great beam of Gull Island lighthouse flashed through the murk, a signal that no one had seen for years, she knew at once that it was a cry for help. She ordered the launch away from the quay, and with a roar of engines the little boat bucked out into the waves and the darkening spray.

Pryce stared at the great beam sweeping across the heaving sea, and for the first time his composure cracked, as he understood exactly what it meant. He seized the brass plate from the table, thrust Isla aside and ran out into the rain toward the jetty where his motorboat strained at its rope. Owen, who had never raced anyone in his life, found that he was running after him.

Owen, quiet accountant that he was, reached the jetty first and planted himself squarely on the narrow boards with his arms spread wide. Pryce rushed him in blind fury, slipped on the streaming planks, and went sprawling, and the brass plate flew from his grasp and rang against the stones like a bell. For a long moment nobody moved, and then Hannah, arriving breathless, put her foot firmly on the evidence.

At that moment the police launch swung alongside the jetty, and Inspector Okoye stepped onto the slick boards, her coat streaming and her expression unreadable. She looked at the brass plate, at the folder in Isla's hands and at the sodden figure of Gideon Pryce, and then she formally arrested him on suspicion of theft and fraud. He opened his mouth to protest, but, for once in his life, no smooth words came.

In the police station in Saltmere, Mabel Cray wept for an hour and then told the whole story, sentence by tangled sentence. She had known for two years that Pryce's clocks were stolen, she confessed, and had carried the boxes and kept the books because she was frightened for her job and for her family. The inspector listened gravely and said that honesty now would count for a great deal, and Mabel promised to give evidence against him.

Guided by Mabel's confession and Isla's copied pages, the police searched a barn that Pryce rented on a lonely farm beyond Thornby. In the farthest corner, wrapped in grey blankets and hidden behind sacks of straw, lay the great turret clock of Saint Brannock's, scratched but whole. Nine other stolen clocks stood in the shadows beside it, each one tagged with a fictitious price.

Back in the kitchen of their house, with the reporters gone and the curtains open at last, Owen told Isla everything about the missing money and then pressed the heavy iron key into her hand. She stared at it, then at him, and her face crumpled into laughter and tears together, for she realised that while she had been hiding from a villain, her husband had been quietly saving her father's dream. They stood a long time without speaking, and in the quiet that followed no further explanation was needed by either of them.

At sunrise the two sisters sat side by side on the sea wall, with the red scarf folded between them and the tide drawing quietly in below. They spoke of their father, of the long year of silence and of the foolish pride that had kept them apart, and each promised, with a laugh that was also a sob, never again to carry a secret alone. The sun climbed over the harbour, and for the first time in a week the whole world felt gently and honestly new.

A week late, but all the brighter for it, the Lantern Festival lit up Saltmere harbour with hundreds of drifting paper lights, and the whole town came out to watch them float. Above the crowd the restored turret clock of Saint Brannock's struck ten, a deep, golden sound that had been missing for months, and Isla, Owen and Hannah stood together and listened. Whatever had vanished in Saltmere that autumn had been found, and what had been mended was worth more than what had been lost.
